outcome: The main conjecture remains open, but a 2025 paper (published in Notes on Number Theory and Discrete Mathematics, also issued as a UNLV master's thesis by the same group) proved additional special cases of the conjecture, for totient values k = 2^t, 2p^s, 2^2 p, and 2pq (p, q distinct primes); no AI involvement is evident in either.
summary: The main conjecture — whether every value of Euler's totient function is attained by at least two integers — is still unresolved as of September 2026. Standard reference sources (the live Wikipedia article and MathWorld) both describe it as open, with the best-known lower bound on any counterexample still Kevin Ford's 1998/1999 result that a counterexample must exceed 10^(10^10) (equivalently, the conjecture is verified/true for all n below that bound); no sharper bound was found in the window. Within the window, a legitimate, peer-reviewed piece of progress appeared: 'On the special cases of Carmichael's totient conjecture' by Shannon, Shiue, He and Saito (Notes on Number Theory and Discrete Mathematics, received May 2025, accepted August 2025, published online 2025-08-15), which is the journal version of Christopher Saito's UNLV master's thesis (deposited 2025-05-15). This work proves the conjecture holds for all n with φ(n) = k in the specific forms k = 2^t, k = 2p^s, k = 2^2 p, and k = 2pq (p, q distinct primes) — a genuine restriction/case of the stated conjecture, so it is classified `partial` with `resolution_direction` `confirmed` (the settled cases go the way the conjecture predicts, i.e. multiplicity > 1 holds for them). Neither the journal article's fetched content nor the thesis abstract mentions any AI-tool assistance in deriving the results, so `ai_role` is `none`. The triage's two flagged items (an academia.edu page claiming a full proof, and a figshare 'note') were checked for accessibility: both academia.edu and figshare returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching, so their content could not be directly read; however, no secondary source, blog, forum, or citation anywhere in web search results treats either as a credible or discussed resolution — no journal acceptance, no expert digestion, no retraction notice, and no citation trail exists for the academia.edu 'proof' or the figshare 'note'. Given that the conjecture is a century-old, well-known open problem that would attract immediate expert attention if genuinely resolved, and given the complete absence of any uptake (no mention on Wikipedia, MathWorld, John D. Cook's number-theory blog which specifically discusses Carmichael's conjecture as recently as October 2025, or elsewhere), these are treated as uncredible/unreviewed amateur claims that do not constitute a resolution and are not separately counted as events. John D. Cook's blog post 'More on Carmethael' (2025-10-09) discusses only the existing verification bound (10^(10^10)) and makes no mention of any new proof, disproof, or AI involvement, corroborating that no headline change to the main conjecture has occurred.
competing_reading: One could argue the academia.edu/figshare claims deserve a `claimed` status entry of their own if their content could be read and shown to contain a genuine (if unreviewed) proof attempt — I could not fetch either page (403 errors) and found no secondary discussion of their content, so I cannot rule out that they contain something more substantive than the total silence around them suggests. However, the complete absence of any citation, discussion, or expert reaction to either item over the roughly 1-3 years they have been online strongly suggests they are not credible, and the correct default per the instructions is to not count an unreviewed, undigested, uncited claim as an event absent stronger evidence.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the academia.edu and figshare documents (e.g. via a logged-in session or an alternate mirror) to check whether they contain any coherent argument, combined with a search for any citations of either work in later papers or any mathematician's public comment on them.
